analysis.one_liner: Bans the federal government and federally funded entities from discriminating for or against anyone based on race.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Act of 2023 was referred to four House committees, received no hearing or vote in any of them, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the federal government, federal contractors, and any state or private entity that receives federal money from discriminating against anyone — or giving anyone a preference — based on race, color, or national origin in contracts, employment, or college admissions [S2][S3]. It would count quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, and timetables as forbidden preferences, wiping out existing race-conscious federal programs like minority-business set-asides [S2]. It would also create a private right of action so individuals could sue violators, including government agencies, and win attorney's fees and back pay [S3]. Agencies would have six months to rewrite their own rules to comply [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People who believe a race-conscious federal program, contract, hiring rule, or admissions policy cost them an opportunity. They could sue in federal court for relief and attorney's fees, and agencies would have to strip preference-based rules from their regulations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People disadvantaged by race-conscious federal programs

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the federal government, its contractors, and recipients of federal aid from intentionally discriminating against, or granting a preference to, any person or group based on race, color, or national origin in contracts, employment, and other federal activities.
Defines a forbidden preference broadly to include quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, timetables, and other numerical objectives, so existing race-conscious federal programs would have to be ended.
Gives any person aggrieved by a violation a private right of action in federal court, with relief including back pay and a mandatory attorney's fee for prevailing plaintiffs.
Requires every federal agency, within six months of enactment, to review and modify its policies and regulations to conform and report the results to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees.

analysis.who_pays: Minority-owned businesses that hold or pursue federal set-aside contracts, and institutions and workers covered by race-conscious hiring, contracting, and admissions programs, would lose those programs. Federal agencies and contractors would bear the cost of rewriting rules and defending against new private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: By defining preference to include set-asides, goals, and timetables, the bill would eliminate existing federal programs designed to expand contracting and employment opportunities for groups historically excluded from them, without any replacement remedy.

A blanket bar on considering race in federal contracting, employment, and admissions applies the same rule to efforts to include and efforts to exclude, meaning race-conscious measures aimed at remedying documented disadvantage would be swept away along with ones that disadvantage people.
The private right of action with mandatory attorney's fees against agencies, contractors, and federally funded entities could generate substantial litigation costs for those organizations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill states a clear principle — the government should not penalize or reward anyone by race — and it gives individuals real enforcement power, which its supporters see as equal protection finally applied to preference programs. The cost is real too: it would dismantle set-asides and numerical goals that many businesses, workers, and schools currently rely on, and it offers nothing in their place. Whether that trade is worth it depends on whether you view existing race-conscious programs as correction or as the problem the bill targets; the bill itself makes no attempt to distinguish between the two.

outcome.mechanism: It went to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever scheduled a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Tiffany introduced the FAIR Act of 2023 on March 9, 2023, with Reps. Burgess Owens, Michelle Steel, and Kat Cammack-listed original cosponsors including Byron Donalds, and it was referred the same day to four committees: Judiciary, Oversight and Accountability, Education and the Workforce, and House Administration.
Eleven cosponsors, all Republicans, signed on during the bill's life.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or floor action is recorded, and the action history ends with the referral, so the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The race-conscious federal programs the bill targeted — including minority-business set-asides and institutions' existing hiring, contracting, and admissions practices — remained in place, benefiting the businesses, workers, and schools that rely on them. Lawmakers who opposed the bill bore no political cost because it never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing federal set-aside programs and their beneficiaries

for.what_they_did: Signed on to the bill, giving it its entire Republican support base.

sides.party_line_note: All eleven cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but the bill never advanced far enough for a chamber vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate set-asides and contracting programs these businesses rely on for federal work, ending a channel they currently depend on. Their interest in keeping those programs runs alongside disadvantaged workers' and communities' interests.

Contractors would be freed from preference-related requirements and goals, but would face new private lawsuits if plaintiffs claim they discriminated or granted preferences. The gain to some contractors comes directly at the expense of firms that currently benefit from set-asides.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities receiving federal aid
industries.note: The bill bars federally funded institutions from considering race in admissions, employment, and contracting, forcing changes for institutions that currently use race-conscious practices while aligning them with a colorblind mandate.
